On the board's reading, Condign's flat denial of any US or Canadian exchange sits oddly with the four redacted lines that follow it, since a complete negative needs no withheld continuation.
The model offices resolve most of what they receive: the Sky Canada report records that only 3.2% of GEIPAN's 3,188 cases remained unidentified after investigation.
The model offices have disagreed with each other: on the 2014 Chilean Navy footage, GEIPAN's analysts proposed an airliner venting wastewater and the Chilean office rejected it.

On the board's reading, Canada in 2025 recommended building the standing public service that Britain abolished in 2009, which Nick Pope argued should not have been closed: two governments moving in opposite directions on the same question.

lead.text: Outside the big national stories, other governments' UFO records mostly show up in someone else's files: a Belgian F-16 intercept in the British archive, a Spanish release noted in a British intelligence study, an Iranian intercept in a US attache's cable. And one G7 government, Canada, has now named the offices it holds up as examples and would partner with: France's GEIPAN, Chile's SEFAA and the US AARO.

record.text: The UK National Archives' guide to the MoD files opened in 2009 says they show the Belgian Air Force scrambling F-16s in March 1990 to intercept UFOs reported by police officers and others, and that an account by General Wilfried de Brouwer, Chief of Operations of the Belgian Air Staff, confirms that the pilots got radar lock-ons but could not explain the phenomena.

The Belgian Air Force sent its official statement to the MoD in November 1993, and the guide places it and de Brouwer's four-page account in named DEFE 24 pieces; a letter from Malcolm Rifkind in the same series says the MoD was not told of the incident at the time and concluded there was no threat to the UK.
The UK's Project Condign study carried Belgian imagery in its Volume 2 figure list, a video frame captioned Belgium 31 March 1990 and a shape comparison for the UK, Russia and Belgium.

Condign Volume 3 records that the Spanish MoD took the phenomenon seriously and reportedly released sixty-six files, which DI 55 staff had not seen, and states that there is no intelligence exchange or collaboration of any sort with the USA and Canada on UFOs, followed by about four redacted lines.

The Tehran intercepts of 19 and 20 September 1976 are known from a US Defense Attache report to DIA, distributed to the Joint Chiefs, the White House, CIA and NSA among others; it names no Iranian aircrew and says its information came from a source's conversation with a sub-source and an F-4 pilot.

The same report records that one F-4 lost instrumentation and communications at 25 nautical miles and that a second got a radar lock at 27 miles, and that the landing area was being checked for radiation; DIA's 1996 search found no further document and no result of that check.

The Sky Canada report describes GEIPAN as three full-time staff with over 20 trained volunteers, and SEFAA as the official Chilean body inside the civil aviation directorate; CEFAA was created by Chile's aviation authority in 1997 and publishes monthly resolved-case bulletins.

The UK MoD stated that Condign's purpose was to judge the value of the reports to defence intelligence, chiefly whether there was any threat to the UK, and to identify any military technologies of interest.

summary.text: The Sky Canada report found no single model or established standard, but named the processes of the United States, France and Chile as examples of coordinated, transparent and scientifically driven approaches; the board treats this as the first time a G7 government has said publicly which arrangements it would copy.

France's GEIPAN is the reference case of a civil state office: published classifications and case conclusions, a national police feed, and a small staff with trained volunteers; Chile's SEFAA is the civil-aviation version of the same model, inside its aviation authority, publishing monthly resolved-case bulletins.

The Belgian wave of 1989-1990 and its F-16 intercept, the Spanish MoD file release, and Japan's review of the 2026 US file release are the other governments that appear on the board mostly through foreign records or press reports.

Brazil's route was different again: its military UFO records were transferred to the national archive and are searchable there, including material on the 1986 incident; and a Brazilian case of 1996 is now the subject of a US congressional records request.
